_meta.purpose: Deterministic applicability matrix: entity type + activities -> which EU regulations apply. No AI, no inference — every verdict is a stated rule with a reason a compliance officer can check against the text.
_meta.scope: Belgium / EU financial services. Covers the 15 regulations held in full article text under data/laws/.

status_values.direct: Directly applicable to this entity type.
status_values.conditional: Applies only if you carry out the relevant activity — check the condition.
status_values.na: Not applicable to this entity type on its own.

_meta.disclaimer: Indicative mapping to orient a compliance officer, not legal advice. Always verify against the instrument and any Belgian transposition.

entities.label: Other obliged entity
entities.desc: Accountant, lawyer, estate agent, trust or company service provider

regulations.name: AMLR

notes.insurer: Life insurance and other investment-related insurance only — non-life insurers are not obliged entities on this basis.
notes.other: Obliged-entity status depends on your specific profession and the thresholds in Art. 3.

regulations.why: Single rulebook for customer due diligence, beneficial ownership and internal controls. Directly applicable — no national transposition.

regulations.name: AMLD6

notes.bank: Binds you through Belgian transposition, not directly — watch for stricter Belgian requirements.
notes.insurer: Life insurance only, mirroring AMLR scope.

regulations.why: Covers supervision, FIUs and beneficial-ownership registers. Reaches you via Belgian law, so the national text is what governs.

regulations.name: AMLA Regulation

notes.bank: Direct AMLA supervision applies only to selected obliged entities operating cross-border at scale. Otherwise AMLA sets the standards and the NBB or FSMA applies them to you.

regulations.why: Establishes the EU AML authority. For most firms the effect is indirect — through the standards your national supervisor then enforces.

regulations.name: TFR

notes.casp: Extends the travel rule to crypto-asset transfers — originator and beneficiary information must accompany every transfer.

regulations.why: The travel rule: information that must accompany transfers of funds and crypto-assets. Applies to payment service providers and CASPs.

regulations.name: DORA

notes.other: DORA lists financial entities specifically — most non-financial obliged entities fall outside it.

regulations.why: ICT risk management, incident reporting, resilience testing and third-party oversight. Its list of 'financial entities' is deliberately broad.

regulations.name: NIS2

notes.bank: DORA is lex specialis for ICT risk in financial entities — where DORA covers a requirement, it displaces the NIS2 equivalent. Belgian transposition still matters for anything DORA leaves open.

regulations.why: Baseline EU cybersecurity regime. For financial entities it largely gives way to DORA, but does not disappear entirely.

regulations.name: MiCA

notes.casp: Full authorisation, conduct, custody and governance regime.
notes.bank: Credit institutions may provide crypto-asset services under their existing licence, subject to notification — the conduct rules still bind.
notes.emi: Issuing an e-money token brings you squarely into MiCA Title IV.

regulations.why: Authorisation and conduct regime for crypto-asset issuers and service providers.

regulations.name: MiFID II
regulations.full_name: Markets in Financial Instruments Directive II

notes.bank: Applies when you provide investment services — suitability, product governance, best execution.
notes.fund: Applies to MiFID 'top-up' services such as individual portfolio management.
notes.casp: Crypto-assets outside MiFID's definition of financial instruments fall under MiCA instead.

regulations.why: Investor protection and conduct-of-business rules for investment services.

regulations.name: MiFIR

notes.invfirm: Transaction reporting, transparency and trading obligations.

regulations.why: Market transparency and transaction reporting. Directly applicable — the regulation half of the MiFID package.

regulations.name: MAR

notes.invfirm: Includes the obligation to detect and report suspicious orders and transactions (STORs).
notes.casp: MiCA carries its own market-abuse title for crypto-assets — MAR does not extend to them.

regulations.why: Insider dealing and market manipulation, including suspicious transaction and order reporting.

regulations.name: CRR

notes.invfirm: Only the largest, bank-like investment firms remain in CRR. Most are under IFR/IFD instead.

regulations.why: Own funds, liquidity, leverage and large exposures for credit institutions.

regulations.name: CRD IV

notes.bank: Authorisation, governance, remuneration and the SREP — reaches you via Belgian banking law.

regulations.why: Authorisation and prudential supervision of credit institutions.

regulations.name: PSD2

notes.bank: Applies to your payment services — strong customer authentication, access to accounts, conduct.
notes.pi: Your core authorisation regime. PSD3 and the PSR are in the legislative pipeline.

regulations.why: Authorisation and conduct for payment services, including strong customer authentication.

regulations.name: EMD2

notes.casp: Issuing an e-money token engages both EMD2 and MiCA Title IV.

regulations.why: Issuance and redeemability of electronic money, and safeguarding of funds.

regulations.name: GDPR

notes.bank: Note the tension between AML record-keeping duties and data-minimisation and erasure rights — document how you reconcile them.

regulations.why: Applies to anyone processing personal data. In practice that is every regulated firm, and it interacts directly with your KYC records.
